newsitem.title: USA: UAW, Ford bargainers to meet through weekend.
newsitem.headline: UAW, Ford bargainers to meet through weekend.

text.p: Bargainers for the United Auto Workers union and Ford Motor Co plan to haggle through the weekend over outsourcing, wages and other issues critical to a new labor agreement for the Big Three U.S. automakers, officials said Friday.
Negotiators are racing to beat a September 14 deadline for contracts covering more than 386,000 UAW workers at Ford, General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp.
"Negotiators seem to be making some good progress on the issues, but we still have a lot of work to do," said Jon Harmon, a Ford spokesman.

A person familiar with the talks said that the UAW wants a return to annual base-wage increases -- it has proposed a two percent annual increase over the life of the contract, which may stretch to four years.

The UAW has worked under three-year contracts for more than 40 years. In recent pacts, workers have received a base wage increase of three percent in the first year and lump-sum bonuses on top of unchanged wage rates in the remaining two years.

The union, which has said its top priority is job security, also has sought to require that Ford replace every single worker who retires over the contract term. In the current pact, it only need to hire one new worker for every two who retire.
Ford has about 104,000 hourly UAW workers in its U.S. plants, while GM has about 216,000 and Chrysler has 66,000.
Thousands of auto workers are expected to retire during the next several years, making the issue of new hires -- how many and at what wage scale -- a critical one in the talks.
"In many ways, they're negotiating on behalf of a lot of people who haven't been hired yet," said Dale Brickner, director of Michigan State University's labor relations department.

In the current contract, new workers start at wages that are only 70 percent of those veteran workers, and it takes three years for them to reach parity. Veteran assemblers at the three companies make wages of $19 an hour, while skilled trades workers make about $22 an hour.
Including health care and other benefits, the total compensation averages $43 an hour for each UAW employee.
Labor analysts say the "grow-in" wage scale has caused rifts between younger and older workers at many plants and will be a major point of discussion in the talks.
A report in Friday editions of the New York Times that Ford has proposed a permanently lower wage scale in any new auto parts business it enters could not be immediately confirmed.
However, the Big Three have long desired a lower wage scale for auto parts workers, who now earn as much as assembly workers.

Automakers have turned increasingly to outside suppliers, who often pay their workers half of what assembly workers make, to help lower their costs. In an effort to limit job losses to such outsourcing moves, the UAW wants automakers to encourage their suppliers to unionize.
